title: Tamper fault that won't clear
summary: The panel keeps reporting a tamper after covers are closed and the system is reset.
symptoms: Tamper shown on the keypad and won't clear or keeps returning.
The system may refuse to arm or need a code to acknowledge.
safety: Tamper is often monitored 24 hours: tell the monitoring centre and the site contact before opening covers or enclosures.
External sirens can sound when their cover or tamper is disturbed — follow the manufacturer's service procedure before opening one.
Only measure resistance on an isolated circuit; disconnect the conductors first and power down where the manufacturer requires.
Don't leave tamper inputs linked out as a permanent fix.
Backup batteries can deliver very high fault currents: never short battery leads or terminals, and isolate the battery as well as mains before working inside a panel or power supply.

Mains (230 V) wiring is restricted electrical work — only a licensed electrician may work on it. Apprentices should do these tests under supervision and within their licence conditions; follow site procedures and the manufacturer's documentation.

nodes.text: Which tamper is the panel reporting?
nodes.help: Check the keypad's alarm/trouble view or the event log for the source.

answers.label: The panel or power supply enclosure
A siren, strobe or expansion module
answers.finding: Tamper reported on a siren or module.

nodes.text: Is the enclosure lid fully closed, with its tamper switch (and any wall/back tamper) pressed in?

answers.label: Yes
answers.finding: Enclosure closed and tamper switch actuated.

answers.label: No
answers.finding: Enclosure lid or tamper switch not seated.

nodes.text: Is the detector's cover fully seated, with the tamper switch pressed?
nodes.help: Look for a cover not clipped on, a bent tamper spring or plunger, or cable pushing the PCB away from the cover.

answers.label: Yes
answers.finding: Detector cover seated, tamper switch pressed.

answers.label: No
answers.finding: Detector cover or tamper switch not seated.

nodes.text: Has the tamper been acknowledged / reset at the keypad since the cover was closed?
nodes.help: Many panels latch tamper alarms until a user or installer code resets them. Check the panel's manual for which code level is needed.

answers.label: No
answers.finding: Tamper not yet reset at the keypad.

review.note: Whether a tamper latches, and which code level clears it, is panel-specific.

nodes.text: How is this detector's tamper wired?
nodes.help: In generic dual EOL the tamper contact is in series with the zone loop. Many sites instead wire tampers to a separate tamper zone or input.

answers.label: In series with the zone loop (generic dual EOL)
answers.finding: Tamper wired in series with the zone loop.

answers.label: To a separate tamper zone or input
answers.finding: Tamper wired to a separate input.

nodes.text: Which EOL resistors does this zone use?
nodes.help: Generic dual EOL wiring: R1, the EOL resistor, in series with the loop; R2, the alarm resistor, across the detector's NC alarm contact; the tamper contact in series. Expected readings are calculated from the values you choose. These are examples, not values for any particular panel — and not every installation uses this wiring. If yours differs, choose 'Different wiring or not sure'.

unsupported.label: Different wiring (e.g. tamper resistor, triple EOL) or not sure
unsupported.finding: EOL wiring not known or not the generic dual EOL topology.

nodes.text: What does the zone loop measure at the panel?

test.procedure: Isolate the zone: disconnect both zone conductors from the panel. With the detector sealed and its cover on, measure across the two conductors on the Ω range.
test.expected: About the sealed reading ({sealed}). With the tamper in series (generic dual EOL), an open tamper reads OL.

nodes.safety: Resistance range only on the disconnected conductors.

ranges.label: Near 0 Ω
ranges.finding: Loop reads {value}: shorted — some panels report this as tamper.

ranges.label: Below the sealed reading
ranges.finding: Loop reads {value}: below the sealed reading.

ranges.label: Above the sealed reading but not open
ranges.finding: Loop reads {value}: above the sealed reading.

ranges.label: OL / open circuit
ranges.finding: Loop reads {value}: open — the tamper or loop is open.

nodes.title: Identify the tamper source first
nodes.summary: Tamper can come from detectors, enclosures, sirens or modules; each is checked differently.
verify: Check the keypad's alarm / trouble view and the event log for the tamper source.
Walk the site for open covers and lids.
actions: Restart this guide once the source is known.

nodes.title: Enclosure tamper not actuated
nodes.summary: A lid or tamper switch that isn't fully pressed keeps the tamper active.
verify: Close the lid fully and check the tamper switch plunger travels far enough.
Check any wall / back tamper is pressed against the mounting surface.
actions: Re-seat the lid, adjust or replace the switch bracket, then reset the tamper at the keypad.

nodes.title: Enclosure tamper circuit
nodes.summary: The lid and switch look right, but the panel still reports tamper. The switch, its wiring, or a latched alarm are possible.
verify: Reset the tamper at the keypad with the required code level.
With power isolated as the manufacturer requires and the switch leads disconnected, check the switch reads closed when pressed and open when released.
Check the tamper input's wiring and plug for loose connections.
actions: Replace a faulty switch or repair the wiring, then reset.
escalate: Contact the manufacturer's support if the input still reports tamper with a known-good switch.

nodes.title: Siren or module tamper
nodes.summary: Siren, strobe and expander tampers have their own switches and loops.
verify: Follow the siren's or module's service procedure before opening it.
Check its cover and tamper switch are seated, and its tamper loop wiring back to the panel.
For modules, check the event log for which device is reporting.
actions: Re-seat covers, repair tamper loop wiring, then reset at the keypad.
notes: External sirens with their own battery can sound when disturbed — warn the site first.

nodes.title: Detector cover or tamper switch
nodes.summary: A cover that isn't fully seated keeps the tamper switch open.
verify: Seat the cover fully; check the tamper spring or plunger isn't bent and cable isn't pushing the PCB.
actions: Re-seat the cover, then reset the tamper at the keypad.

nodes.title: Reset the latched tamper
nodes.summary: The cover is closed, but many panels hold a tamper until it's acknowledged.
verify: Reset / acknowledge the tamper at the keypad with the required code level.
If it returns straight away, restart this guide and answer 'Yes' to the reset question.
actions: Reset the tamper and confirm the zone shows sealed.

nodes.title: Confirm the zone's EOL values first
nodes.summary: This guide can only judge readings for the generic dual EOL wiring with known resistor values.
verify: Check the zone's EOL type and values in the panel programming or installation records.
actions: Restart this guide once you know the expected values.

nodes.title: The loop is open
nodes.summary: With the cover closed the loop still reads open. In generic DEOL an open loop is usually reported as tamper.
verify: At the detector, with the zone isolated, measure across the tamper switch terminals with the cover pressed: it should read close to 0 Ω.
If the switch is fine, follow the 'Alarm zone permanently open' guide to find the open.
actions: Replace a faulty tamper switch or detector, or repair the open conductor.

nodes.title: The loop is shorted
nodes.summary: Some panels report a short as tamper.
verify: Follow the 'Alarm zone permanently shorted' guide.

review.note: Whether this panel reports a shorted dual EOL loop as tamper is panel-specific.

nodes.title: The loop reads outside the expected bands
nodes.summary: Some panels report readings outside their sealed and alarm bands as tamper.
verify: Measure each EOL resistor on its own with the zone isolated.
Check joints for corrosion.
Confirm the panel's programmed EOL values and how it reports out-of-band readings.
actions: Fit the correct resistors, remake poor joints or correct programming, then reset.

nodes.title: Loop is sealed — check the panel
nodes.summary: Isolated, the loop reads sealed, yet the tamper persists. A latched alarm, programming or the panel input are likely.
verify: Reconnect the zone and reset the tamper with the correct code level.
Check the zone's EOL programming matches the wiring.
Fit a known-good resistor equal to R1 (the sealed reading) on the input, zone conductors disconnected, and check the status.
actions: Correct programming; report the input if it misreads a known-good resistor.
escalate: Contact the manufacturer's support if the input misreads a known-good resistor.

nodes.title: Measurements needed
nodes.summary: Without a loop measurement the cause can't be narrowed down safely.
verify: Get a multimeter: the next step is an isolated resistance measurement.
actions: Return to this guide with a meter.

nodes.title: Check the separate tamper loop
nodes.summary: The tamper has its own input, so the zone loop isn't the place to look. Test the tamper loop itself.
verify: Isolate the tamper loop (disconnect it at the panel) and measure it on the Ω range with the cover pressed home.
Compare the reading with what the panel's documentation says that tamper input expects (a closed loop, or a specific resistor).
Check the switch on its own: close to 0 Ω when pressed, OL when released.
actions: Repair the loop or replace the switch, then reset the tamper at the keypad.

review.note: What a separate tamper input expects (closed loop, or its own resistor) is panel-specific.

nodes.title: Find out how the tamper is wired
nodes.summary: Whether the tamper is in the zone loop or on its own input decides what to measure.
verify: Check the detector's terminals and the panel's zone list or programming.
Check installation records or as-built drawings.
actions: Restart this guide once you know how the tamper is wired.

cover.title: Cover or lid not seated
cover.detail: The tamper switch isn't pressed because the cover, lid or mounting isn't fully home.

tamper-switch.title: Faulty tamper switch
tamper-switch.detail: The switch doesn't close when pressed.

tamper-wiring.title: Tamper wiring fault
tamper-wiring.detail: Open or loose conductor in the tamper loop or plug.

latched.title: Tamper latched in the panel
latched.detail: The panel holds the tamper until it's acknowledged with the right code level.

cable.title: Cable fault
cable.detail: Open or shorted conductor between the panel and the detector.

wrong-resistor.title: Wrong resistor value
wrong-resistor.detail: Loop reads outside the panel's bands.

config.title: Programming doesn't match the wiring
config.detail: EOL type or values in the panel don't match what's installed.

panel-input.title: Panel input fault
panel-input.detail: The input misreads a healthy loop.

escalation: Contact the manufacturer's support if the input misreads a known-good resistor or switch.
If a tamper must be left isolated, tell the site contact and monitoring centre, record it, and book the return visit. Never leave it linked out permanently.
notes: Panels differ in how they report open, short and out-of-band readings — some show them as tamper, others as trouble or alarm. Check the panel's documentation.
2k2 / 4k4 and 10k / 20k are generic examples, not manufacturer specifications.

pending: The ±10 % band used to call a reading 'about' the expected value allows for 5 % resistors, cable resistance and meter accuracy. It is a diagnostic aid, not any panel's alarm threshold — confirm it suits long cable runs.
Expected readings assume the generic dual EOL topology (R1 in series, R2 across the NC alarm contact, tamper in series). Confirm against the panel's and detector's wiring diagrams.
Tamper latching and reset code levels are panel-specific.
Siren and module service procedures are manufacturer-specific.
